_sentence","paragraphIndex":57},{"text":"Because the response of any cortical taste cell is ambiguous, the meaning requires a comparison across cells A given papilla may contain up to 10 or more taste buds, and each taste bud contains about 50 receptor cells.","In adult humans, taste buds lie mainly along the edge of the tongue.","Then try it again on the edge of your tongue and notice the taste. It begins when airborne chemicals contact receptor membranes within the nose, and it contributes strongly to food flavor as well as to detecting biologically important cues.","Kalat discusses smell as both a sensory and behavioral system: olfactory information can influence food selection, avoidance reactions, and social responses.","Chemicals reaching the nasal receptor surfaces activate olfactory receptors. Like metabotropic neurotransmitter receptors, each olfactory receptor protein traverses the cell membrane seven times and responds to a chemical outside the cell (an odorant molecule) by triggering changes in a G protein inside the cell.","Olfactory receptors are vulnerable to damage because they are exposed to the air.","Each olfactory neuron axon contains copies of its olfactory receptor protein, which it uses like an identification card to find its correct partner.","However, if the entire olfactory surface is damaged at once by a blast of toxic fumes so that the system has to replace all the receptors at the same time, many of them fail to make the correct connections, and olfactory experience does not fully recover.","The diversity of olfactory receptors makes possible narrow specialization of functions.","Each olfactory cell has only one receptor type, and most receptors respond to either just one chemical or several closely related chemicals.","Some receptors respond synergistically; that is, they respond to a combination of two chemicals, but hardly at all to either one alone. Fast and slow muscle fibers and proprioceptive feedback contribute to different kinds of action."},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Not all movements are controlled in the same way: some depend heavily on feedback, while others unfold in learned sequences. Use the book’s categories to distinguish voluntary, involuntary, and feedback-sensitive movements."},{"type":"heading","id":"bp14-m7-1-study-1","text":"Muscles generate force, circuits coordinate it"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Movement depends on contractions of muscle fibers governed by motor neurons. Muscle fibers can differ in speed and endurance, making some more suited to rapid forceful actions and others to sustained activity. The nervous system must regulate both which muscles contract and how their activity is timed. Movements are not simply a sequence of commands from a single central controller; sensory feedback and distributed circuits continuously influence them."},{"type":"heading","id":"bp14-m7-1-study-2","text":"Feedback and proprioception"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Proprioceptors supply information about muscle stretch, tension, and body position. Reflex pathways can respond to changes before conscious awareness, helping stabilize posture and adjust ongoing movement. Feedback is especially useful when a task is slow enough for incoming information to guide corrections. Fast movements often require advance planning because feedback arrives too late to control every moment. A movement can therefore blend feedforward commands with feedback-based adjustments."},{"type":"heading","id":"bp14-m7-1-study-3","text":"Voluntary, involuntary, and skilled actions"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Some movements occur through reflex mechanisms, others through habitual patterns, and others are strongly guided by deliberate goals. These are not wholly isolated categories: walking, for example, involves ongoing spinal and brain processes as well as conscious decisions about destination or obstacles. Repeated behavior can become organized into useful sequences, making action more efficient. Learning changes the connections between perception, goals, and muscle control."},{"type":"heading","id":"bp14-m7-1-study-4","text":"Units of analysis"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Study movement at multiple levels: a muscle fiber contracts, a motor unit recruits fibers, spinal circuits coordinate local responses, and brain systems organize action in context. The physical result depends on the body's mechanics and what sensory information is available. This hierarchical view is more useful than memorizing muscles independently of the behavior they produce."},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m7-1-h01","text":"Muscles and Movements"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Smooth muscles control the digestive system and other organs, skeletal or striated muscles control movement of the body in relation to the environment, and cardiac muscles control the heart.","sourcePrintedPage":226,"sourcePdfPage":244,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Although each muscle fiber receives information from only one axon, a given axon may innervate more than one muscle fiber.","sourcePrintedPage":226,"sourcePdfPage":244,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The eye muscles have a ratio of about one axon per three muscle fibers, and the biceps muscles of the arm have a ratio of one axon to more than a hundred fibers .","sourcePrintedPage":226,"sourcePdfPage":244,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"A neuromuscular junction is a synapse between a motor neuron axon and a muscle fiber.","sourcePrintedPage":226,"sourcePdfPage":244,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"An axon at a skeletal muscle releases acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction, causing a muscle contraction.","sourcePrintedPage":226,"sourcePdfPage":244,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"There is no message to cause relaxation or to move a muscle in the opposite direction.","sourcePrintedPage":226,"sourcePdfPage":244,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Moving a leg or arm back and forth requires opposing sets of muscles, called antagonistic muscles .","sourcePrintedPage":226,"sourcePdfPage":244,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m7-1-h02","text":"Fast and Slow Muscles"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Your temperature is the same as the water around you, and because muscle contractions are chemical processes, they slow down in the cold.","sourcePrintedPage":228,"sourcePdfPage":246,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"You have to use more muscles, but you swim at about the same speed .","sourcePrintedPage":228,"sourcePdfPage":246,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"In colder water, the fish uses more white muscles, maintaining its speed but fatiguing faster.","sourcePrintedPage":228,"sourcePdfPage":246,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Human and other mammals have various kinds of muscle fibers mixed together, not in separate bundles as in fish.","sourcePrintedPage":228,"sourcePdfPage":246,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Our muscles range from fast-twitch fibers with fast contractions and rapid fatigue to slow-twitch fibers with less vigorous contractions and no fatigue .","sourcePrintedPage":228,"sourcePdfPage":246,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"We rely on our slow-twitch and intermediate fibers, like a fish’s red muscles, for the least strenuous activities, such as walking leisurely or talking.","sourcePrintedPage":228,"sourcePdfPage":246,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Slow-twitch fibers do not fatigue because they are aerobic — they use oxygen during their movements.","sourcePrintedPage":228,"sourcePdfPage":246,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"People vary in their percentages of fast-twitch and slow-twitch fibers, for reasons based on both genetics and training.","sourcePrintedPage":228,"sourcePdfPage":246,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"To endure this ordeal, contestants need many adaptations of their muscles and metabolism, such as increasing numbers of mitochondria .","sourcePrintedPage":228,"sourcePdfPage":246,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"In contrast, competitive sprinters have more fast-twitch fibers and other adaptations for speed instead of endurance .","sourcePrintedPage":228,"sourcePdfPage":246,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m7-1-h03","text":"Muscle Control by Proprioceptors"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"A proprioceptor (from the Latin proprius , meaning “one’s own”) is a receptor that detects the position or movement of a body part—in these cases, a muscle.","sourcePrintedPage":229,"sourcePdfPage":247,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Muscle proprioceptors detect the stretch and tension of a muscle and send messages that enable the spinal cord to adjust its signals.","sourcePrintedPage":229,"sourcePdfPage":247,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"When the muscle is stretched, the muscle spindle sends a message to a motor neuron in the spinal cord, which in turn sends a message back to the muscle, causing a contraction .","sourcePrintedPage":229,"sourcePdfPage":247,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The nerves from the spindles send action potentials to the motor neuron in the spinal cord, which sends action potentials to contract the extensor muscle and straighten the leg.","sourcePrintedPage":229,"sourcePdfPage":247,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Golgi tendon organs , proprioceptors in the tendons at opposite ends of a muscle, respond to increases in muscle tension.","sourcePrintedPage":229,"sourcePdfPage":247,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Golgi tendon organs detect the tension that results during a muscle contraction, sending messages to the spinal cord to inhibit the motor neurons.","sourcePrintedPage":229,"sourcePdfPage":247,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The proprioceptors not only control important reflexes but also provide the brain with information.","sourcePrintedPage":229,"sourcePdfPage":247,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The actual weight displaces their proprioceptors less than expected and therefore yields the perception of a lighter object.","sourcePrintedPage":230,"sourcePdfPage":248,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m7-1-h04","text":"Units of Movement"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Movements include speaking, walking, threading a needle, and throwing a basketball while off balance and evading two defenders.","sourcePrintedPage":230,"sourcePdfPage":248,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Different kinds of movement need different kinds of control by the nervous system.","sourcePrintedPage":230,"sourcePdfPage":248,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m7-1-h05","text":"Voluntary and Involuntary Movements"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"We generally think of reflexes as involuntary because they are insensitive to reinforcements, punishments, and motivations.","sourcePrintedPage":230,"sourcePdfPage":248,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"One example is the stretch reflex, and another is the constriction of the pupils in response to bright light.","sourcePrintedPage":230,"sourcePdfPage":248,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"When a person walks, which we think of as a voluntary activity, reflexes compensate for the bumps and irregularities in the road.","sourcePrintedPage":230,"sourcePdfPage":248,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Keep your foot moving while you draw the number 6 in the air with your right hand.","sourcePrintedPage":230,"sourcePdfPage":248,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"It is difficult to make “voluntary” clockwise and counterclockwise movements on the same side of the body at the same time.","sourcePrintedPage":230,"sourcePdfPage":248,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"However, it is typically much less difficult to move your left hand in one direction while moving the right foot in the opposite direction.","sourcePrintedPage":230,"sourcePdfPage":248,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m7-1-h06","text":"Movements Varying in Sensitivity to Feedback"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The military distinguishes ballistic missiles from guided missiles.","sourcePrintedPage":230,"sourcePdfPage":248,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"A ballistic missile is launched like a thrown ball: Once it is launched, no one can change its aim.","sourcePrintedPage":230,"sourcePdfPage":248,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"A guided missile detects the target and adjusts its trajectory to correct its aim.","sourcePrintedPage":230,"sourcePdfPage":248,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Similarly, some movements are ballistic, and others are corrected by feedback.","sourcePrintedPage":230,"sourcePdfPage":248,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"A ballistic movement , such as a reflex, is executed as a whole, but most behaviors are subject to feedback correction.","sourcePrintedPage":230,"sourcePdfPage":248,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"When a person threads a sewing needle, they make a slight movement, check their aim, and then readjust.","sourcePrintedPage":230,"sourcePdfPage":248,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Similarly, a singer who holds a single note hears any wavering of the pitch and corrects it.","sourcePrintedPage":230,"sourcePdfPage":248,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m7-1-h07","text":"Sequences of Behaviors"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Many rapid sequences of behaviors depend on central pattern generators , neural mechanisms in the spinal cord that generate rhythmic patterns of motor output.","sourcePrintedPage":230,"sourcePdfPage":248,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"include the mechanisms that generate wing flapping in birds, fin movements in fish, and the “wet-dog shakes.” The stimulus that activates a central pattern generator does not control the rhythm of the movements.","sourcePrintedPage":231,"sourcePdfPage":249,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"For example, a cat scratches itself at a rate of three to four strokes per second, regardless of what caused the scratching.","sourcePrintedPage":231,"sourcePdfPage":249,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Cells in the lumbar segments of the spinal cord generate this rhythm, and they can do so even if they are isolated from the brain or if the muscles are paralyzed .","sourcePrintedPage":231,"sourcePdfPage":249,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"For example, a mouse periodically grooms itself by sitting up, licking its paws, wiping them over its face, closing its eyes as the paws pass over them, licking the paws again, and so forth.","sourcePrintedPage":231,"sourcePdfPage":249,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"A set of cells in the medulla produces this sequence of actions .","sourcePrintedPage":231,"sourcePdfPage":249,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m7-1-h08","text":"In Closing: Categories of Movement"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"A motor neuron and its associated muscle participate in a great many kinds of movements, and we need many brain areas to control them.","sourcePrintedPage":231,"sourcePdfPage":249,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"A chicken with featherless wings makes the same movements, even though the featherless wings will not break the chicken’s fall .","sourcePrintedPage":231,"sourcePdfPage":249,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"A yawn includes a prolonged open-mouth inhalation, often accompanied by stretching, and a shorter exhalation.","sourcePrintedPage":231,"sourcePdfPage":249,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Yawns are consistent in duration, with a mean of just under 6 seconds.","sourcePrintedPage":231,"sourcePdfPage":249,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Certain facial expressions are also programmed, such as smiles, frowns, and the raised-eyebrow greeting.","sourcePrintedPage":231,"sourcePdfPage":249,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Hugging is not a built-in motor program, but it is interesting to note that the average nonromantic hug lasts 3 seconds for people throughout the world .","sourcePrintedPage":231,"sourcePdfPage":249,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"bullet","text":"The difference allows the eye to move more precisely than the biceps.","headingId":"bp14-m7-1-h01","sourcePrintedPage":226,"sourcePdfPage":244},{"type":"bullet","text":"At your elbow, for example, your flexor muscle brings your hand toward your shoulder and your extensor muscle straightens the arm.","headingId":"bp14-m7-1-h01","sourcePrintedPage":226,"sourcePdfPage":244},{"type":"bullet","text":"Your only defense against predators is your ability to swim away.","headingId":"bp14-m7-1-h02","sourcePrintedPage":228,"sourcePdfPage":246},{"type":"bullet","text":"If you run up a steep hill at full speed, you switch to fast-twitch fibers that fatigue rapidly.","headingId":"bp14-m7-1-h02","sourcePrintedPage":228,"sourcePdfPage":246},{"type":"bullet","text":"Low glucose activates a gene that stops the muscles from using glucose, switching you to the fast-twitch muscles that depend on anaerobic use of fatty acids.","headingId":"bp14-m7-1-h02","sourcePrintedPage":228,"sourcePdfPage":246},{"type":"bullet","text":"If you walk along a bumpy road, you might set your foot down a little too hard or not quite hard enough.","headingId":"bp14-m7-1-h03","sourcePrintedPage":229,"sourcePdfPage":247},{"type":"bullet","text":"When a muscle is stretched, the spinal cord sends a signal to contract it reflexively.","headingId":"bp14-m7-1-h03","sourcePrintedPage":229,"sourcePdfPage":247},{"type":"bullet","text":"One kind of proprioceptor is the muscle spindle, a receptor parallel to the muscle that responds to a stretch.","headingId":"bp14-m7-1-h03","sourcePrintedPage":229,"sourcePdfPage":247},{"type":"bullet","text":"Note that this reflex provides negative feedback: When a person sets a foot down on a bump on the road, their knee bends a bit, stretching the extensor muscles of that leg.","headingId":"bp14-m7-1-h03","sourcePrintedPage":229,"sourcePdfPage":247},{"type":"bullet","text":"Some muscles are so strong that they could damage themselves if too many fibers contracted at once.","headingId":"bp14-m7-1-h03","sourcePrintedPage":229,"sourcePdfPage":247},{"type":"bullet","text":"In doing so, they put on the brakes to prevent an excessive contraction.","headingId":"bp14-m7-1-h03","sourcePrintedPage":229,"sourcePdfPage":247},{"type":"bullet","text":"For example, you might try a golf ball and a larger ball of the same weight.","headingId":"bp14-m7-1-h03","sourcePrintedPage":230,"sourcePdfPage":248},{"type":"bullet","text":"(Watching is essential.) Then remove it and drop the other object onto the same hand.","headingId":"bp14-m7-1-h03","sourcePrintedPage":230,"sourcePdfPage":248},{"type":"bullet","text":"Try this: While sitting, raise your right foot and make clockwise circles.","headingId":"bp14-m7-1-h05","sourcePrintedPage":230,"sourcePdfPage":248},{"type":"bullet","text":"You will probably reverse the direction of your foot movement.","headingId":"bp14-m7-1-h05","sourcePrintedPage":230,"sourcePdfPage":248},{"type":"bullet","text":"Even a mouse without forelimbs goes through the same sequence, so we understand that it does not depend on sensory feedback.","headingId":"bp14-m7-1-h07","sourcePrintedPage":231,"sourcePdfPage":249},{"type":"bullet","text":"By comparing species, we observe that a motor program can be gained or lost through evolution.","headingId":"bp14-m7-1-h07","sourcePrintedPage":231,"sourcePdfPage":249},{"type":"bullet","text":"Charles Sherrington described a motor neuron in the spinal cord as “the final common path.” He meant that regardless of what sensory and motivational processes occupy the brain, the result is either a muscle contraction or its inhibition.","headingId":"bp14-m7-1-h08","sourcePrintedPage":231,"sourcePdfPage":249},{"type":"bullet","text":"Chickens, of course, still have the genetic programming to fly.","headingId":"bp14-m7-1-h08","sourcePrintedPage":231,"sourcePdfPage":249},{"type":"bullet","text":"On the other hand, ostriches, emus, and rheas, which have not used their wings for flight in millions of generations, have lost the genes for flight movements and do not flap their wings when dropped.","headingId":"bp14-m7-1-h08","sourcePrintedPage":231,"sourcePdfPage":249},{"type":"bullet","text":"We generally think of reflexes as involuntary because they are insensitive to reinforcements, punishments, and motivations.","headingId":"bp14-m7-1-h04","sourcePrintedPage":230,"sourcePdfPage":248},{"type":"bullet","text":"A ballistic missile is launched like a thrown ball: Once it is launched, no one can change its aim.","headingId":"bp14-m7-1-h04","sourcePrintedPage":230,"sourcePdfPage":248},{"type":"bullet","text":"Many rapid sequences of behaviors depend on central pattern generators , neural mechanisms in the spinal cord that generate rhythmic patterns of motor generate force, circuits coordinate it","text":"Movement depends on contractions of muscle fibers governed by motor neurons. Muscle fibers can differ in speed and endurance, making some more suited to rapid forceful actions and others to sustained activity. The nervous system must regulate both which muscles contract and how their activity is timed. Movements are not simply a sequence of commands from a single central controller; sensory feedback and distributed circuits continuously influence them.","kind":"companion_original_explanation","sourcePrintedStart":226,"sourcePrintedEnd":232,"sourcePdfStart":244,"sourcePdfEnd":250},{"id":"bp14-m7-1-study-2","title":"Feedback and proprioception","text":"Proprioceptors supply information about muscle stretch, tension, and body position. Reflex pathways can respond to changes before conscious awareness, helping stabilize posture and adjust ongoing movement. Feedback is especially useful when a task is slow enough for incoming information to guide corrections. Fast movements often require advance planning because feedback arrives too late to control every moment. A movement can therefore blend feedforward commands with feedback-based adjustments.","kind":"companion_original_explanation","sourcePrintedStart":226,"sourcePrintedEnd":232,"sourcePdfStart":244,"sourcePdfEnd":250},{"id":"bp14-m7-1-study-3","title":"Voluntary, involuntary, and skilled actions","text":"Some movements occur through reflex mechanisms, others through habitual patterns, and others are strongly guided by deliberate goals. These are not wholly isolated categories: walking, for example, involves ongoing spinal and brain processes as well as conscious decisions about destination or obstacles. Repeated behavior can become organized into useful sequences, making action more efficient. Learning changes the connections between perception, goals, and muscle control.","kind":"companion_original_explanation","sourcePrintedStart":226,"sourcePrintedEnd":232,"sourcePdfStart":244,"sourcePdfEnd":250},{"id":"bp14-m7-1-study-4","title":"Units of analysis","text":"Study movement at multiple levels: a muscle fiber contracts, a motor unit recruits fibers, spinal circuits coordinate local responses, and brain systems organize action in context. These systems contribute to planning, executing, adjusting, and inhibiting movements."},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The connections between motor activity and cognition are important here. Compare how the cortex, cerebellum, and basal ganglia contribute, rather than attributing movement to a single motor center."},{"type":"heading","id":"bp14-m7-2-study-1","text":"Planning and selection"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Premotor and related cortical regions help organize actions before and during execution. Motor cortex influences descending pathways that reach the spinal cord, but movement preparation also includes deciding whether to act. Prefrontal processes help with goals and inhibition: holding back an impulsive movement can be part of successful control. The nervous system considers expected outcomes, current sensory conditions, and learned habits when selecting an action."},{"type":"heading","id":"bp14-m7-2-study-2","text":"Descending signals and spinal circuits"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Commands from the brain reach motor systems through multiple routes, including pathways that influence voluntary limb movement and others important for posture or orienting. The spinal cord is not a passive cable: its circuits organize reflexes and patterns of coordinated muscle activity. Damage at different points in this chain can produce distinct patterns of weakness, loss of control, or altered reflexes."},{"type":"heading","id":"bp14-m7-2-study-3","text":"Cerebellum and basal ganglia"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The cerebellum contributes to timing, coordination, adjustment, and learning of skilled movements. It compares expected and actual consequences and helps refine performance. Basal ganglia circuits have important roles in initiating or selecting actions and regulating their vigor and sequence. The two systems cooperate with cortex but do not perform identical jobs. This distinction becomes especially clear in movement disorders, where the kind of impaired movement depends on the affected network."},{"type":"heading","id":"bp14-m7-2-study-4","text":"Mirror neurons and conscious decisions"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Certain neurons respond both during an action and during observation of similar actions, prompting hypotheses about action understanding. Those hypotheses need careful evaluation: a neural response alone does not prove a sweeping explanation of empathy, imitation, or social behavior. Studies of movement preparation also show that brain activity can precede a person's report of consciously deciding to act. That finding raises questions about timing and awareness without simply settling the philosophical debate about free will."},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m7-2-h01","text":"The Cerebral Cortex"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Axons from the motor cortex do not go directly to the muscles, but to the brainstem and spinal cord, which send impulses to the muscles .","sourcePrintedPage":234,"sourcePdfPage":252,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Although each hemisphere mainly controls the muscles on the contralateral side, both hemispheres contribute to planning movements on both sides .","sourcePrintedPage":234,"sourcePdfPage":252,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The cerebral cortex is necessary for complex actions such as talking or writing, but not for coughing, sneezing, gagging, laughing, or crying .","sourcePrintedPage":234,"sourcePdfPage":252,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The lack of cerebral control may explain why it is hard to perform those actions represents coordinated movements, not just single muscle contractions.","sourcePrintedPage":234,"sourcePdfPage":252,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"For many twitches.","sourcePrintedPage":234,"sourcePdfPage":252,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Later researchers found different results when they lengthened the spinal cord and other areas to find the right combination of muscles .","sourcePrintedPage":235,"sourcePdfPage":253,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Researchers sometimes use fMRI to measure brain responses while people are posterior parietal cortex is active during the delay, evidently preparing the movement .","sourcePrintedPage":236,"sourcePdfPage":254,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The supplementary motor cortex in the prefrontal cortex is also essential for planning and organizing movements.","sourcePrintedPage":236,"sourcePdfPage":254,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"After mild electrical stimulation of the supplementary motor cortex, people report an urge or desire to make a movement, and after stronger stimulation, they actually make a movement .","sourcePrintedPage":236,"sourcePdfPage":254,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Activity in the supplementary motor cortex begins at least a second before the start of a voluntary movement and builds up gradually .","sourcePrintedPage":236,"sourcePdfPage":254,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"It receives information about the target to which the body is directing its movement, as well as information about the body’s current position and posture .","sourcePrintedPage":236,"sourcePdfPage":254,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Both kinds of information are necessary to direct a movement toward a target.","sourcePrintedPage":236,"sourcePdfPage":254,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Parts of the prefrontal cortex are important for considering the probable outcomes of movements .","sourcePrintedPage":236,"sourcePdfPage":254,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m7-2-h03","text":"Inhibiting a Movement"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Or you start to swing at a tennis ball in a doubles match when your partner shouts, “let it go,” because it will land out of bounds.","sourcePrintedPage":236,"sourcePdfPage":254,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"In cases like these, two brain areas are sending competing messages, and the outcome depends on whether the stop message arrives in time to cancel the action message .","sourcePrintedPage":237,"sourcePdfPage":255,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Another example—not an important behavior for its own sake, but a convenient one for psychologists to study— is the antisaccade task .","sourcePrintedPage":237,"sourcePdfPage":255,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"A saccade (sa-KAHD) is a voluntary eye movement from one target to another.","sourcePrintedPage":237,"sourcePdfPage":255,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"People generally agree that it is easier to look at the finger that moved than the finger that didn’t.","sourcePrintedPage":237,"sourcePdfPage":255,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Before age 5 to 7 years, most children find it almost impossible to look away from the wiggling finger.","sourcePrintedPage":237,"sourcePdfPage":255,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"That is, the brain prepares to inhibit the unwanted action and substitute a different one.","sourcePrintedPage":237,"sourcePdfPage":255,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m7-2-h04","text":"Mirror Neurons"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"A discovery in neuroscience that excited many psychologists was mirror neurons , which are active both during a movement and while watching someone else perform the same movement .","sourcePrintedPage":237,"sourcePdfPage":255,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Mirror neurons were first reported in the premotor cortex of monkeys and later in other areas and other species, including humans .","sourcePrintedPage":237,"sourcePdfPage":255,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The theoretical interest comes from the possibility that we use mirror neurons to understand other people or to identify with them.","sourcePrintedPage":237,"sourcePdfPage":255,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"One speculation was that a lack of mirror neurons might be responsible for autism or schizophrenia, disorders associated with deficient social relationships.","sourcePrintedPage":237,"sourcePdfPage":255,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"If mirror neurons are going to explain imitation or empathy, the mirror neurons would have to come first.","sourcePrintedPage":237,"sourcePdfPage":255,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The only evidence for inborn mirror neurons came from reports that some newborn infants imitate certain adult facial expressions, such as tongue protrusion.","sourcePrintedPage":237,"sourcePdfPage":255,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"A review of the literature over decades found that six research groups have reported positive findings, whereas 10 groups have not .","sourcePrintedPage":237,"sourcePdfPage":255,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Mirror neurons are activated not only by seeing an action but also by any reminder of the action, such as hearing an action or reading about it .","sourcePrintedPage":237,"sourcePdfPage":255,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m7-2-h05","text":"From the Brain to the Spinal Cord"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Messages from the brain must reach the medulla and spinal cord, which control the muscles.","sourcePrintedPage":237,"sourcePdfPage":255,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Paths from the cerebral cortex to the spinal cord are called the corticospinal tracts .","sourcePrintedPage":237,"sourcePdfPage":255,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The lateral corticospinal tract extends from the primary motor cortex, nearby areas of the cortex, and the","sourcePrintedPage":238,"sourcePdfPage":256,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The medial corticospinal tract extends from many areas of the cerebral cortex, as well as from several areas of the midbrain and medulla (Figure 7.11).","sourcePrintedPage":239,"sourcePdfPage":257,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Axons of the medial tract go to both sides of the spinal cord about equally, where they control the muscles of the neck, shoulders, and trunk and therefore movements as walking, turning, bending, standing up, and sitting down .","sourcePrintedPage":239,"sourcePdfPage":257,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"An easy way to remember the functions of the lateral and medial tracts is that the lateral tract controls muscles in the lateral parts of the body, such as hands and feet.","sourcePrintedPage":239,"sourcePdfPage":257,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Note that both paths cross in the medulla and that the touch information arrives at brain areas side by side with those areas responsible for motor control.","sourcePrintedPage":239,"sourcePdfPage":257,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"For example, someone with impaired control of the hand muscles might move the shoulders and trunk in a way that repositions the hand.","sourcePrintedPage":239,"sourcePdfPage":257,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m7-2-h06","text":"The Cerebellum"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The term cerebellum is Latin for “little brain.” Decades ago, most texts described the function of the cerebellum as “balance and coordination.” Well, yes, people with cerebellar damage do lose balance and coordination, but that description understates the importance of this structure.","sourcePrintedPage":239,"sourcePdfPage":257,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The cerebellum has more neurons than the rest of the brain combined , a huge number of synapses, and many functions.","sourcePrintedPage":239,"sourcePdfPage":257,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The cerebellum is essential for any behavior that relates to aim or precise timing of short intervals.","sourcePrintedPage":239,"sourcePdfPage":257,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Here is a quick way to test the cerebellum: Hold up your hands and ask someone to look at one hand and then quickly look to the other hand.","sourcePrintedPage":239,"sourcePdfPage":257,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"This move function depends on the cerebellar cortex (the surface of the cerebellum), which sends messages to the cerebellar nuclei (clusters of cell bodies) in the interior of the cerebellum (Figure 7.13).","sourcePrintedPage":240,"sourcePdfPage":258,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"This hold function depends on the nuclei alone .","sourcePrintedPage":240,"sourcePdfPage":258,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Finally, the finger moves to the nose by a slower movement that does not depend on the cerebellum.","sourcePrintedPage":240,"sourcePdfPage":258,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"A police officer testing someone for drunkenness may use the finger-to-nose test or similar tests because the cerebellum is one of the first brain areas that alcohol affects.","sourcePrintedPage":240,"sourcePdfPage":258,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m7-2-h07","text":"Cellular Organization"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The cerebellum receives input from the spinal cord, from the sensory systems, and from the cerebral cortex.","sourcePrintedPage":240,"sourcePdfPage":258,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Processing in the cerebellum finally reaches the cerebellar nuclei, which send output back to the cerebral cortex as well as to downstream targets (Figure 7.14).","sourcePrintedPage":240,"sourcePdfPage":258,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m7-2-h08","text":"Functions Other than Movement"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Traditionally, the cerebellum has been emphasized for its role in movement, but it has reciprocal connections with all parts of the cerebral cortex, enabling it to contribute to almost everything the brain does .","sourcePrintedPage":242,"sourcePdfPage":260,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The chapter on learning and memory will discuss the role of the cerebellum in classical conditioning.","sourcePrintedPage":242,"sourcePdfPage":260,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"In one study, people were told to keep their eyes fixated on a central point.","sourcePrintedPage":242,"sourcePdfPage":260,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"At various times, they would see the letter E on either the left or right half of the screen, and they were to indicate the direction in which it was oriented (E,","sourcePrintedPage":242,"sourcePdfPage":260,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Because the circuit diagram of cells in the cerebellum is nearly uniform throughout, researchers and theorists have tried to describe a single function for the cerebellum, but so far without notable success.","sourcePrintedPage":242,"sourcePdfPage":260,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Perhaps it is no more reasonable to seek “the” function of the cerebellum than to seek “the” function of the cerebral cortex .","sourcePrintedPage":242,"sourcePdfPage":260,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m7-2-h09","text":"The Basal Ganglia"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The direct pathway from the striatum inhibits the globus pallidus, which inhibits part of the thalamus.","sourcePrintedPage":243,"sourcePdfPage":261,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Neuroscientists long believed that the direct pathway stimulates movements whereas the indirect pathway inhibits them.","sourcePrintedPage":243,"sourcePdfPage":261,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"However, later evidence found that both pathways are active before a movement and neither is active when the animal is at rest .","sourcePrintedPage":243,"sourcePdfPage":261,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"A popular hypothesis is that the direct pathway enhances the selected movement whereas the indirect pathway inhibits competing movements .","sourcePrintedPage":243,"sourcePdfPage":261,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"This path inhibits actions quickly, when it is important to change plans suddenly .","sourcePrintedPage":243,"sourcePdfPage":261,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"In trials when it heard a signal indicating exactly when to move, the basal ganglia exhibited little activity.","sourcePrintedPage":243,"sourcePdfPage":261,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"In another study, people used a computer mouse to draw lines on a screen while researchers used PET scans to examine brain activity.","sourcePrintedPage":243,"sourcePdfPage":261,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Activity in the basal ganglia increased when people drew a new line but not when they traced a line already on the screen .","sourcePrintedPage":243,"sourcePdfPage":261,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Because cells in the primary motor cortex become active before those in the basal ganglia, the basal ganglia must not be responsible for selecting which movement to make.","sourcePrintedPage":244,"sourcePdfPage":262,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Many cells in the basal ganglia cells respond strongly to signals indicating that a response will probably lead to reward.","sourcePrintedPage":244,"sourcePdfPage":262,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Separate sections of the basal ganglia respond to the recent value associated with a stimulus and the long-term average value associated with it .","sourcePrintedPage":244,"sourcePdfPage":262,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Cells in the basal ganglia store longterm memories of the reward value of many objects, more than 90 in one study .","sourcePrintedPage":244,"sourcePdfPage":262,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m7-2-h10","text":"Conscious Decisions and Movement"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Each of us has the feeling, “I consciously decide to do something, and then I do it.” It seems so obvious that we might not even question it, but research casts doubt on this assumption.","sourcePrintedPage":244,"sourcePdfPage":262,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"On the average, people report that their decision to move occurred about 200 ms before the actual movement. (The decision occurred then.","sourcePrintedPage":244,"sourcePdfPage":262,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"People report it later.) For example, if you reported that your decision to move occurred at position 25, your decision came 200 ms before the movement that began at position 30. (Remember, the light moves around the circle in 2.56 seconds.) However, your motor cortex produces a kind of activity called a","sourcePrintedPage":244,"sourcePdfPage":262,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"readiness potential for any voluntary movement, and on average, the readiness potential begins at least 500 ms before the movement.","sourcePrintedPage":245,"sourcePdfPage":263,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The research has been replicated in other laboratories, so the results are solid .","sourcePrintedPage":245,"sourcePdfPage":263,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"One study found that some neurons in the supplementary motor cortex begin activating more than a second before the reported time of the decision .","sourcePrintedPage":245,"sourcePdfPage":263,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Many have assumed that if people can accurately state the time of a stimulus or a movement, they are equally accurate at stating the time of a conscious decision.","sourcePrintedPage":245,"sourcePdfPage":263,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Remember, the letters changed only twice a second, so it wasn’t possible to determine the time of decision with great accuracy.","sourcePrintedPage":246,"sourcePdfPage":264,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"However, it wasn’t necessary, because parts of the frontal and parietal cortices showed activity specific to the left or right hand 7 to 10 seconds before the response .","sourcePrintedPage":246,"sourcePdfPage":264,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"heading","id":"deep-bp14-m7-2-h11","text":"In Closing: Movement Control and Cognition"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"It is tempting to describe behavior in three steps—first we perceive, then we think, and finally we act.","sourcePrintedPage":246,"sourcePdfPage":264,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"The cerebellum has traditionally been considered a major part of the motor system, but it is now known to be important in timing sensory processes.","sourcePrintedPage":246,"sourcePdfPage":264,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"People with basal ganglia damage are slow to start a movement, and they are also slow at making any kind of choice.","sourcePrintedPage":246,"sourcePdfPage":264,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Organizing a movement is not something we tack on at the end of our thinking.","sourcePrintedPage":246,"sourcePdfPage":264,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"develops gradually, because the movement is self-initiated, the type that depends on the basal ganglia .","sourcePrintedPage":246,"sourcePdfPage":264,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"paragraph","text":"Human infants are at first limited to gross movements of the trunk, arms, and legs.","sourcePrintedPage":247,"sourcePdfPage":265,"sourceMethod":"selected_textbook_sentence"},{"type":"bullet","text":"Since the pioneering work of Gustav Fritsch and Eduard Hitzig (1870), neuroscientists have known that direct electrical stimulation of the primary motor cortex — the precentral gyrus of the frontal cortex, just anterior to the central sulcus—elicits movements.","headingId":"bp14-m7-2-h01","sourcePrintedPage":234,"sourcePdfPage":252},{"type":"bullet","text":"Controlling movement also depends on connections between the cortex and subcortical areas, as illustrated in Figure 7.9.","headingId":"bp14-m7-2-h01","sourcePrintedPage":234,"sourcePdfPage":252},{"type":"bullet","text":"Figure 7.10 (which repeats parts of Figure 3.23) depicts which areas of the somatosensory cortex feel parts of the body, and which areas of the motor cortex control parts of the body.","headingId":"bp14-m7-2-h01","sourcePrintedPage":234,"sourcePdfPage":252},{"type":"bullet","text":"For example, some of the cells in the hand area control grasping movements and others control movements to release a grip.","headingId":"bp14-m7-2-h01","sourcePrintedPage":234,"sourcePdfPage":252},{"type":"bullet","text":"Stimulation of one spot caused a monkey to make a grasping movement with its hand, move its hand to just in front of the mouth, and open its mouth— as if it were picking up something and preparing to eat it.","headingId":"bp14-m7-2-h01","sourcePrintedPage":235,"sourcePdfPage":253},{"type":"bullet","text":"Physicians sometimes perform brain surgery on people who are awake, anesthetizing only the skin of the scalp.","headingId":"bp14-m7-2-h02","sourcePrintedPage":235,"sourcePdfPage":253},{"type":"bullet","text":"The details vary, but the general idea is that people detect a first signal that tells them what they are supposed to do, and then they wait for a second signal that indicates make the movement now.","headingId":"bp14-m7-2-h02","sourcePrintedPage":235,"sourcePdfPage":253},{"type":"bullet","text":"It is also essential for inhibiting a habitual movement when you want to do something else, and for learning to correct errors of movement.","headingId":"bp14-m7-2-h02","sourcePrintedPage":236,"sourcePdfPage":254},{"type":"bullet","text":"When you imagine how a movement would feel, you activate your premotor cortex.","headingId":"bp14-m7-2-h02","sourcePrintedPage":236,"sourcePdfPage":254},{"type":"bullet","text":"If you had damage to this area, many of your movements would be disorganized, such as showering with your clothes on or pouring water on the tube of toothpaste instead of the toothbrush.","headingId":"bp14-m7-2-h02","sourcePrintedPage":236,"sourcePdfPage":254},{"type":"bullet","text":"If you do something absentminded first thing in the morning, probably your prefrontal cortex is not fully awake.","headingId":"bp14-m7-2-h02","sourcePrintedPage":236,"sourcePdfPage":254},{"type":"bullet","text":"Consider what happens when you need to restrain an impulse.","headingId":"bp14-m7-2-h03","sourcePrintedPage":236,"sourcePdfPage":254},{"type":"bullet","text":"The traffic light changes from red to green, but just as you are about to drive forward, you hear an ambulance siren telling you to stay out of the way.","headingId":"bp14-m7-2-h03","sourcePrintedPage":236,"sourcePdfPage":254},{"type":"bullet","text":"Suppose a person is staring straight ahead when something to one side or the other moves.","headingId":"bp14-m7-2-h03","sourcePrintedPage":237,"sourcePdfPage":255},{"type":"bullet","text":"Performance declines in old age and as a result of schizophrenia, attention-deficit disorder, or alcohol intoxication.","headingId":"bp14-m7-2-h03","sourcePrintedPage":237,"sourcePdfPage":255},{"type":"bullet","text":"For example, certain neurons become active both when people smile and when they see someone else smile.","headingId":"bp14-m7-2-h04","sourcePrintedPage":237,"sourcePdfPage":255},{"type":"bullet","text":"That result suggests built-in mirror neurons that connect the sight of a movement to the movement itself.","headingId":"bp14-m7-2-h04","sourcePrintedPage":237,"sourcePdfPage":255},{"type":"bullet","text":"After some practice, these “mirror” neurons turned into “counter-mirror” neurons that responded to moving one finger and watching a different finger.","headingId":"bp14-m7-2-h04","sourcePrintedPage":237,"sourcePdfPage":255},{"type":"bullet","text":"We have two such tracts, the lateral and medial corticospinal tracts.","headingId":"bp14-m7-2-h05","sourcePrintedPage":237,"sourcePdfPage":255},{"type":"bullet","text":"Diseases of the spinal cord impair movement, as listed in Table 7.1.","headingId":"bp14-m7-2-h05","sourcePrintedPage":238,"sourcePdfPage":256},{"type":"bullet","text":"In bulges of the medulla called pyramids, the lateral tract crosses to the contralateral side of the spinal cord.","headingId":"bp14-m7-2-h05","sourcePrintedPage":238,"sourcePdfPage":256},{"type":"bullet","text":"You may be able to move your fingers on just one side of the body, but movements such as standing, sitting, or turning necessarily include both sides.","headingId":"bp14-m7-2-h05","sourcePrintedPage":239,"sourcePdfPage":257},{"type":"bullet","text":"Figure 7.12 compares the lateral tract to the spinal pathway bringing touch information to the cortex.","headingId":"bp14-m7-2-h05","sourcePrintedPage":239,"sourcePdfPage":257},{"type":"bullet","text":"For a person to control their hands, they have to know where they are and what they are doing now.","headingId":"bp14-m7-2-h05","sourcePrintedPage":239,"sourcePdfPage":257},{"type":"bullet","text":"If a stroke damages the primary motor cortex of one hemisphere, the result is impaired movement on the other side of the body.","headingId":"bp14-m7-2-h05","sourcePrintedPage":239,"sourcePdfPage":257},{"type":"bullet","text":"It receives input from the cerebral cortex, especially the frontal and parietal lobes, and relays information back to modify cortical activity.","headingId":"bp14-m7-2-h06","sourcePrintedPage":239,"sourcePdfPage":257},{"type":"bullet","text":"People with cerebellar damage can accurately judge the loudness of a sound, but not its duration.","headingId":"bp14-m7-2-h06","sourcePrintedPage":239,"sourcePdfPage":257},{"type":"bullet","text":"The eyes make many short movements until, by trial and error, they eventually find the intended spot.","headingId":"bp14-m7-2-h06","sourcePrintedPage":240,"sourcePdfPage":258},{"type":"bullet","text":"In the finger-to-nose test, someone is instructed to hold one arm straight out and then, at command, touch the nose as quickly as possible.","headingId":"bp14-m7-2-h06","sourcePrintedPage":240,"sourcePdfPage":258},{"type":"bullet","text":"Figure 7.15 is a simplified diagram of neurons in the cerebellum.","headingId":"bp14-m7-2-h07","sourcePrintedPage":240,"sourcePdfPage":258},{"type":"bullet","text":"Sometimes, they saw a signal telling where the letter would be on the screen.","headingId":"bp14-m7-2-h08","sourcePrintedPage":242,"sourcePdfPage":260},{"type":"bullet","text":"For most people, that signal improved their performance even if it appeared just 100 ms before the letter.","headingId":"bp14-m7-2-h08","sourcePrintedPage":242,"sourcePdfPage":260},{"type":"bullet","text":"The cerebellum contributes to many tasks that have little to do with one another.","headingId":"bp14-m7-2-h08","sourcePrintedPage":242,"sourcePdfPage":260},{"type":"bullet","text":"The term basal ganglia applies to the subcortical forebrain structures illustrated in Figure 7.16.","headingId":"bp14-m7-2-h09","sourcePrintedPage":242,"sourcePdfPage":260},{"type":"bullet","text":"( Ganglia is the plural of ganglion.) These structures include the caudate nucleus, the putamen (pyuh-TAY-men), the globus pallidus, and the nucleus accumbens.","headingId":"bp14-m7-2-h09","sourcePrintedPage":242,"sourcePdfPage":260},{"type":"bullet","text":"The illustration shows the direct and indirect pathways of the basal ganglia.","headingId":"bp14-m7-2-h09","sourcePrintedPage":243,"sourcePdfPage":261},{"type":"bullet","text":"For example, a monkey in one study was trained to move a hand left or right to receive food.","headingId":"bp14-m7-2-h09","sourcePrintedPage":243,"sourcePdfPage":261},{"type":"bullet","text":"Again, the basal ganglia seem critical for selfinitiated actions, not for stimulus-elicited actions.","headingId":"bp14-m7-2-h09","sourcePrintedPage":243,"sourcePdfPage":261},{"type":"bullet","text":"If someone shouts, “Time for dinner,” you get up at once and head for the table.","headingId":"bp14-m7-2-h09","sourcePrintedPage":243,"sourcePdfPage":261},{"type":"bullet","text":"Describing the role of the basal ganglia in these terms makes sense of what we see in patients with damage to the basal ganglia, as in Parkinson’s disease.","headingId":"bp14-m7-2-h09","sourcePrintedPage":244,"sourcePdfPage":262},{"type":"bullet","text":"People with basal ganglia damage are impaired at learning motor skills and converting them into smooth, automatic responses.","headingId":"bp14-m7-2-h09","sourcePrintedPage":244,"sourcePdfPage":262},{"type":"bullet","text":"You don’t choose which movement to make, but you choose the time freely.","headingId":"bp14-m7-2-h10","sourcePrintedPage":244,"sourcePdfPage":262},{"type":"bullet","text":"NOW!” You note where the spot was at that critical instant and report, “I made my decision when the light was at position 25.” The researchers compare your report to their records of your brain activity and your wrist movement.","headingId":"bp14-m7-2-h10","sourcePrintedPage":244,"sourcePdfPage":262},{"type":"bullet","text":"In this example, it would start when the light was at position 18, as illustrated in Figure 7.19.","headingId":"bp14-m7-2-h10","sourcePrintedPage":245,"sourcePdfPage":263},{"type":"bullet","text":"The results seem to indicate that your conscious decision does not cause your action.","headingId":"bp14-m7-2-h10","sourcePrintedPage":245,"sourcePdfPage":263},{"type":"bullet","text":"Rather, you become conscious of the decision after the process leading to action has been underway for about 300 milliseconds.","headingId":"bp14-m7-2-h10","sourcePrintedPage":245,"sourcePdfPage":263},{"type":"bullet","text":"Someone monitoring your cortex could, in this situation, predict your choice a few seconds before you were aware of making the decision.","headingId":"bp14-m7-2-h10","sourcePrintedPage":246,"sourcePdfPage":264},{"type":"bullet","text":"Nevertheless, your brain activity does not always start 7 to 10 seconds before you make a movement.","headingId":"bp14-m7-2-h10","sourcePrintedPage":246,"sourcePdfPage":264},{"type":"bullet","text":"It is intimately intertwined with all of our sensory and cognitive processes.","headingId":"bp14-m7-2-h11","sourcePrintedPage":246,"sourcePdfPage":264},{"type":"bullet","text":"The study of movement is not just the study of muscles.","headingId":"bp14-m7-2-h11","sourcePrintedPage":246,"sourcePdfPage":264},{"type":"bullet","text":"When you report the time of the decision, it may be little more than a guess.","headingId":"bp14-m7-2-h11","sourcePrintedPage":246,"sourcePdfPage":264},{"type":"bullet","text":"Reporting when you decided to make a voluntary movement is like reporting when you fell in love with someone: You know when you were sure of it, or when you first said, “I love you,” but the process was developing gradually long before that.","headingId":"bp14-m7-2-h11","sourcePrintedPage":246,"sourcePdfPage":264},{"type":"bullet","text":"The ability to move one finger at a time matures gradually over at least the first year.","headingId":"bp14-m7-2-h11","sourcePrintedPage":247,"sourcePdfPage":265}],"topicIds":["bp14-m7-2-h01","bp14-m7-2-h02","bp14-m7-2-h03","bp14-m7-2-h04","bp14-m7-2-h05","bp14-m7-2-h06","bp14-m7-2-h07","bp14-m7-2-h08","bp14-m7-2-h09","bp14-m7-2-h10","bp14-m7-2-h11"],"studySections":[{"id":"bp14-m7-2-study-1","title":"Planning and selection","text":"Premotor and related cortical regions help organize actions before and during execution. Motor cortex influences descending pathways that reach the spinal cord, but movement preparation also includes deciding whether to act. Prefrontal processes help with goals and inhibition: holding back an impulsive movement can be part of successful control. The nervous system considers expected outcomes, current sensory conditions, and learned habits when selecting an action.","kind":"companion_original_explanation","sourcePrintedStart":233,"sourcePrintedEnd":248,"sourcePdfStart":251,"sourcePdfEnd":266},{"id":"bp14-m7-2-study-2","title":"Descending signals and spinal circuits","text":"Commands from the brain reach motor systems through multiple routes, including pathways that influence voluntary limb movement and others important for posture or orienting. The spinal cord is not a passive cable: its circuits organize reflexes and patterns of coordinated muscle activity.
